questions.q: Why are learning rate and weight decay typically swept on a log scale rather than a linear scale?
options: Log scale is required by the W&B YAML schema for any numeric parameter
Their effect on training is roughly multiplicative, so the difference between 1e-5 and 1e-4 matters as much as between 1e-3 and 1e-2
Log scale always produces a smaller search space than linear scale
Linear scale cannot represent values smaller than 1.0
questions.explain: Learning rate and weight decay affect training multiplicatively, so a log-uniform distribution spreads samples evenly across orders of magnitude instead of wasting most samples in one narrow region, as a linear-uniform distribution would.

questions.q: Which hyperparameters are the best candidates to include in a sweep's search space?
options: Architecture choices like layer count, since sweeping them is cheap
Every hyperparameter in the config, to be thorough
Hyperparameters where there is real uncertainty about the right value, such as learning rate, weight decay, and dropout
Only hyperparameters that have a discrete set of values
questions.explain: Architecture choices with strong prior evidence are usually fixed rather than swept. Sweep slots are best reserved for hyperparameters with genuine uncertainty, since search cost grows quickly with dimensionality.

questions.q: What happens to Bayesian optimization's sample efficiency as the number of swept dimensions grows past roughly 10-15?
options: It improves, because more dimensions give the optimizer more signal
It stays constant regardless of dimensionality
It degrades — there isn't enough signal per additional trial to localize the optimum
Bayesian optimization becomes equivalent to grid search at any dimensionality
questions.explain: Even though Bayesian search handles higher dimensions better than grid search, its sample efficiency still degrades past roughly 10-15 dimensions, which is why sweeps should focus on a small number of parameters that actually matter.

questions.q: What does an early-termination policy like Hyperband do during a sweep?
options: It stops the entire sweep once the compute budget is exhausted
It kills clearly underperforming runs partway through training, freeing compute for more promising configurations
It automatically widens the search space if no good result is found
It converts a Bayesian search into a grid search after a fixed number of trials
questions.explain: Hyperband and similar policies (like ASHA) terminate runs early once they show clearly underperforming trends, reallocating compute toward configurations that are actually promising rather than letting every run finish.

questions.q: In the W&B sweep workflow, what is the role of `wandb agent` as distinct from `wandb sweep`?
options: wandb agent registers the search space; wandb sweep executes training runs
wandb sweep registers the search space and returns a sweep ID; wandb agent is the worker that pulls a configuration and runs training
They are interchangeable commands that do the same thing
wandb agent only works with grid search, never with Bayesian search
questions.explain: wandb sweep takes the YAML config and registers the sweep, returning an ID. wandb agent is launched (potentially many times, across workers) to pull a configuration from that sweep and actually execute a training run.
